name: Camera angle / eye dominance selection
lead: Camera angle and eye dominance selection is the practice of choosing which side of the face, and which angle and distance, to present to a camera so that a person's features photograph at their best. People use it to look more symmetric, more balanced and better proportioned in photos, video calls and dating-profile pictures, sometimes with reference to a dominant eye.

Research on facial symmetry reports that faces are not perfectly symmetric: on average the eyes, nose and mouth sit slightly to the left relative to the ears, so the right side of the face appears larger [1]. Symmetry increases attractiveness ratings, more so for female faces [1]. This gives the practice its rationale: showing the side or angle that reads as more symmetric or better proportioned.

Distance and lens also change how a face is captured. Photography references note that close camera distances with wide-angle lenses make the nose look large relative to the rest of the face, while stepping back and using a moderate telephoto length produces a flatter, more even look [4]. A 2018 study in JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery modelled that a selfie from about 12 inches makes the base of the nose look roughly 30% wider and the tip about 7% wider than a portrait from five feet [5].

Ocular dominance is the tendency to prefer visual input from one eye; about 70% of people are right-eye dominant and 29% left-eye dominant, and it is mainly studied for aiming tasks [2]. Some people use it as a rule for choosing a side to show; no published study links eye dominance to a flattering camera side.

Beyond distance, portrait photographers describe lens length, lighting direction and focus point as the levers that change how a face reads, and surgeons have documented patients bringing close-up selfies as the reference for what they want changed [9][10]. This article covers the face-side, distance and lens ideas that circulate in looksmaxxing communities and what is known about each.

paras: The face is systematically offset: the eyes, nose and mouth are on average slightly left relative to the ears. This aurofacial asymmetry is about 2 degrees at birth and about 0.5 degrees in adults. During speech, 76% of people show greater mouth movement on the right side.[1]
Researchers caution that mirroring one half of a face to create a symmetric image can produce artificial features, such as an oversized or undersized nose.[1]

Symmetry and averageness make independent contributions to attractiveness ratings, and researchers have tested this with composite faces and mirrored face halves, though the conclusions from mirroring are disputed [1]. Evolutionary hypotheses include the idea that symmetry signals developmental stability or health, and an alternative view that it reflects a lack of prenatal stressors, such as alcohol exposure, rather than superior genes; symmetric faces are rated as healthier, and asymmetry has been found to correlate with physiological and emotional distress [1]. The axial twist theory predicts the average leftward offset of facial features, though its embryological mechanism has not been demonstrated [1].

Eye dominance is only loosely analogous to handedness, and the dominant eye and dominant hand often differ. It can shift with gaze direction, task and fatigue. Tests include the Miles and Porta tests, the Dolman method and lens fogging.[2] The article notes that dominance matters for aiming sports and monovision contact lenses, and that fMRI shows brain activity differences in face perception by dominance, which concern how faces are processed and not how they look.[2]

Perspective distortion is the best-documented camera factor. Close distance with a wide-angle lens enlarges whatever is nearest the lens, typically the nose, and can distort expression; moderate telephoto focal lengths of roughly 85 to 135 mm on a 35 mm camera are described as flattering for portraits [4]. The JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery model compared a 12-inch selfie with a five-foot portrait and reported the nose-base and nose-tip widening above; the senior author described a selfie as a 'portable funhouse mirror' [5]. The authors noted that they did not test whether the distortion drives people to seek surgery [6].
A perception experiment found that recognition of unfamiliar faces in pictures was affected by perspective transformation tied to camera distance [6].

Wikipedia's selfie article describes phone selfies as taken close to the face with wide-angle front lenses, which causes extension distortion that slims the face overall while exaggerating the nose and chin, and recommends a distance of about 5 feet (1.5 m) to reduce distortion [8]. The article reports that an American Academy of Facial Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery survey found 42 percent of surgeons said patients sought surgery to look better in photos, especially close-up selfies [8].
A 2013 study in the journal Laterality asked whether the advent of the camera changed the side of the face that artists chose to show in self-portraits.[3]

A study by Bruno and Bertamini at the University of Parma, described in Wikipedia's selfie article, found that non-professional selfies show a slight bias toward the taker's left cheek, matching patterns in portrait painting and possibly reflecting brain lateralisation; the same group found untrained selfie-takers do not spontaneously follow the rule of thirds [8]. These findings concern which side people tend to show, not which side is more attractive.

sections.h: History of the selfie and camera framing
paras: Self-portraiture on camera is old: Wikipedia lists Robert Cornelius's 1839 daguerreotype self-portrait, the portable Kodak Brownie in 1900, a 1934 photograph taken with a stick described as the original selfie stick, and Buzz Aldrin's 1966 spacewalk selfie [8]. Front-facing cameras appeared on the Game Boy Camera in 1998 and a Kyocera camera phone in 1999, the iPhone 4's front camera helped popularise selfies internationally in 2010, and Oxford Dictionaries named selfie its 2013 word of the year [8]. Close wide-angle front cameras turned the question of which distance and angle to use into an everyday one, and a minor genre of advice about camera angles followed, including the looksmax.org guide on video calls [7].

Portrait photography references describe classic head-and-shoulders focal lengths of about 75 to 135 mm on 35 mm format, noting that telephoto compression tends to be flattering while shorter lenses used from closer can make the nose look larger and the ears smaller [9]. Very long lenses flatten perspective further but make direction and conversation harder, and the article suggests about 200 mm as a practical upper limit for portraits [9].

Lighting changes apparent structure as much as angle. In three-point lighting the key light is typically placed 30 to 60 degrees from the camera with fill on the opposite side; butterfly (Paramount) lighting puts the key above and in front of the camera; and window light and reflectors are common ways to soften shadows [9]. Wide apertures isolate the subject but can leave parts of the face out of focus, and photographers describe stopping down a stop or two with focus on the eyes to keep the whole face sharp [9].

These conventions are the practical counterpart of the distance findings: they let people reduce nose enlargement, control shadow under the brow and jaw, and keep the eyes sharp, which is what many looksmaxxing guides aim for when they discuss angles.

The 2018 study behind the 30 percent figure was led by Boris Paskhover, a facial plastic and reconstructive surgeon at Rutgers New Jersey Medical School, with Stanford computer scientists; the team built a mathematical model using average head and facial measurements from a diverse group of participants, and Paskhover said more research was needed to determine whether the distortion leads frequent selfie-takers to seek surgery [5][6].

The term Snapchat dysmorphia, coined by British cosmetic surgeon Tijion Esho and covered in the press in February 2018, describes patients who arrive asking to look like their filtered selfies. Wikipedia reports that a 2022 survey of the American Academy of Facial Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery found 79 percent of surgeons saw patients seeking changes to look better in selfies, that filters can smooth skin, narrow noses and enlarge eyes, and that a 2019 JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery study linked social media and photo-editing app use with greater acceptance of cosmetic surgery [10]. Platforms banned filters that directly promoted cosmetic surgery in August 2020 [10].

No studies found on choosing a camera side by eye dominance. Related research covers facial asymmetry and attractiveness [1], the orientation artists chose for self-portraits [3], face recognition under perspective changes [6] and modelled selfie-distance distortion [5].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, camera angle is discussed as a way to control how the face reads on video calls and in photos, including how phone distance and height change the look of the nose, eyes and jawline [7].

claims.claim: Holding the phone at certain heights and cutting off part of the face on screen can hide lens distortion and emphasise eyes and jawline.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org guide recommends framing so the midface is partly out of shot and the lower-angle view emphasises the jaw, and a reply says a lower phone position makes profile shots show more forward growth [7].
claims.experts: Photography references and the selfie-distance model report that short distances enlarge the nose and distort proportions [4][5]; no study has tested the specific framing tactics described.

claims.claim: A person's 'good side' can be chosen by facial asymmetry.
claims.believers: Posters say one side of the face looks better and that showing it improves photos.
claims.experts: Facial symmetry research reports small average left-right offsets and higher attractiveness ratings for symmetric faces; it does not state that a particular side is preferred [1].

claims.claim: The dominant eye determines the best camera side.
claims.believers: Some people choose the side matching their dominant eye.
claims.experts: Ocular dominance research concerns aiming and vision tasks [2]; no published study links it to a flattering camera side.

claims.claim: Selfies and close-up video calls distort the nose and midface, so distance and device choice matter.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org guide advises using a laptop camera over a phone camera on video calls because it reduces distortion, and a reply complains that barrel distortion can make faces look unflattering [7].
claims.experts: The JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery model reports roughly 30 percent wider nose base at 12 inches versus five feet [5], and Wikipedia reports similar figures and a 5-foot recommendation [8].

claims.claim: Soft, high-angle or window light and a longer lens make the face look slimmer and more defined.
claims.believers: Photo-advice and looksmaxxing guides recommend stepping back and using a longer lens or laptop camera for flatter, more even proportions [7].
claims.experts: Portrait photography references describe 75 to 135 mm lenses and controlled key and fill lighting as flattering conventions [9]; no study has measured attractiveness ratings across these setups.

claims.claim: Filtered selfies set unrealistic references for how one's face should look.
claims.believers: Surgeons who coined the term Snapchat dysmorphia say patients bring edited selfies as targets [10].
claims.experts: Surgeon surveys and a 2019 study link photo-editing app use with acceptance of cosmetic surgery; causation is not established [10].

card.summary: Picking a 'better side' for photos; faces are measurably asymmetric, but no source links eye dominance to a flattering angle.
card.note: Research covers general facial asymmetry; eye dominance as a selection rule is untested.

quick.overview:
Many people photograph from a preferred side of the face, and some tie that choice to eye dominance.
Faces are known to be slightly asymmetric on average, but neither side is known to be preferred, and no evidence links eye dominance to a flattering angle.
quick.mechanism: People pick the side or angle they judge as more symmetric or flattering. Eye dominance is the preference for one eye's visual input, about 70% right-dominant.
quick.risks: No physical risks. The practice is untested for effect on perceived attractiveness.

chain: Pick the side, angle and distance that read as most symmetric and proportioned
Reduces close-up lens distortion and shows preferred features
Face photographs more balanced and attractive
angle.text: Choosing a camera side, tilt and distance changes which features dominate the image. Practitioners step back from the lens, favour the side they find more symmetric and adjust height and tilt to emphasise the eyes and jawline in photos and video calls.
